slides.narration: The current from a wall socket in India reverses its direction a hundred times every second. In this part we learn to describe such an alternating current by its peak, frequency and phase, find its mean and root mean square values, and see how resistors, coils and capacitors behave on an alternating supply, alone and joined in series.

slides.heading: Sinusoidal AC: period, frequency and phase
slides.body_md:
A sinusoidal current is written
$$i = I_0\sin(\omega t + \phi_0), \qquad \omega = 2\pi f = \dfrac{2\pi}{T}$$
$I_0$ is the **peak value**, $T$ the **period**, $f$ the **frequency** and $(\omega t + \phi_0)$ the **phase**.
bullets: A **phasor** is a vector of length $I_0$ turning anticlockwise at $\omega$; its projection on a fixed line gives the instantaneous value.
Two quantities of the same frequency differ in phase by a fixed angle $\phi$; the one whose phasor is ahead **leads**.
Indian mains: 230 V (rms), $f = 50$ Hz, so $T = 20$ ms and $\omega \approx 314$ rad s$^{-1}$.

slides.narration: A sinusoidal current swings between plus and minus its peak value. One full swing takes the period T, and the frequency f is the number of swings each second. A neat way to picture it is a phasor: an arrow of length equal to the peak, turning anticlockwise. Its height at any instant is the value of the current. Two such arrows at a fixed angle show a phase difference.

slides.heading: Mean value over a half cycle
slides.body_md:
Over a **full** cycle the positive and negative halves cancel, so the mean current is zero. The useful mean is over a **half** cycle:
$$\bar I = \dfrac{1}{T/2}\int_0^{T/2} I_0\sin\omega t\,dt = \dfrac{2I_0}{\omega T}\Big[-\cos\omega t\Big]_0^{T/2} = \dfrac{2I_0}{\pi}$$
bullets: $\bar I = 2I_0/\pi \approx 0.637\,I_0$; likewise $\bar V = 2V_0/\pi$.
It gives the charge carried in one half cycle, $\bar I \times T/2$: the shaded area under the curve.

slides.narration: If we average an alternating current over a whole cycle, the forward and backward halves cancel and we always get zero, which tells us nothing. So the mean value is taken over one half cycle. Integrating the sine curve over half a period gives two I nought over pi, about nought point six three seven of the peak. The shaded area equals this mean times half the period.

slides.heading: The root-mean-square (rms) value
slides.body_md:
The **rms value** is the steady current that gives the same heating in a resistor as the AC. Heating depends on $i^2$:
$$\overline{i^2} = \dfrac{1}{T}\int_0^T I_0^2\sin^2\omega t\,dt = \dfrac{I_0^2}{T}\int_0^T \dfrac{1 - \cos 2\omega t}{2}\,dt = \dfrac{I_0^2}{2}$$
$$I_\text{rms} = \sqrt{\overline{i^2}} = \dfrac{I_0}{\sqrt2} \approx 0.707\,I_0, \qquad V_\text{rms} = \dfrac{V_0}{\sqrt2}$$
bullets: AC meters (hot-wire, moving-iron) read **rms** values; "230 V mains" means $V_\text{rms} = 230$ V, so $V_0 \approx 325$ V.
The factor $1/\sqrt2$ holds only for **sinusoidal** waves.

y.label: value as a fraction of the peak

visual.alt: One cycle of sine omega t and of its square: the sine is negative for half the cycle, but its square is never negative and averages exactly one half over the cycle
visual.caption: Mean of i² = I₀²/2, so I_rms = I₀/√2.

slides.narration: Heating depends on the square of the current, and the square is never negative. Over a cycle, sine squared averages exactly one half, so the mean of i squared is I nought squared over two. The root of that mean is the rms value, I nought over root two. When we say the mains is two hundred and thirty volts, we mean its rms value; its peak is about three hundred and twenty five volts.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: an electric kettle
slides.body_md: A kettle rated 1.2 kW works on 230 V, 50 Hz mains. Find the peak voltage, the rms and peak currents, the mean current over a half cycle, and the period.
bullets: $V_0 = \sqrt2 \times 230 \approx 325$ V; $I_\text{rms} = \dfrac{P}{V_\text{rms}} = \dfrac{1200}{230} \approx 5.22$ A.
$I_0 = \sqrt2 \times 5.22 \approx 7.38$ A; $\bar I = \dfrac{2I_0}{\pi} = \dfrac{2 \times 7.38}{\pi} \approx 4.70$ A.
$T = \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{50} = 0.020$ s $= 20$ ms. (The rating uses rms values: $P = V_\text{rms}I_\text{rms}$.)

slides.narration: The peak voltage is root two times two hundred and thirty, about three hundred and twenty five volts. The rms current is the power over the rms voltage, twelve hundred over two hundred and thirty, about five point two two amperes, so the peak current is about seven point three eight amperes. The half cycle mean is two over pi of that, about four point seven amperes, and the period is twenty milliseconds.

slides.narration: Put each element on its own across an alternating supply. In a resistor the current rises and falls exactly in step with the voltage. In a coil the current trails a quarter of a cycle behind. In a capacitor it runs a quarter of a cycle ahead. The coil and the capacitor oppose the current with reactances, measured in ohms, which change with frequency.

slides.heading: Pure inductor: the current lags by 90°
slides.body_md:
The applied voltage balances the back emf: $V_0\sin\omega t = L\dfrac{di}{dt}$. Integrating,
$$i = -\dfrac{V_0}{\omega L}\cos\omega t = I_0\sin\left(\omega t - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right), \qquad I_0 = \dfrac{V_0}{\omega L}$$
So $i$ **lags** $v$ by $\pi/2$, and the **inductive reactance** is $X_L = \omega L = 2\pi fL$.
bullets: $X_L \propto f$: a coil passes low frequencies easily and **chokes** high ones; for steady DC, $X_L = 0$.

points.label: i peaks a quarter cycle later

visual.alt: Voltage across a pure inductor and the current in it over one cycle: the current reaches each peak a quarter of a cycle after the voltage, so it lags by 90 degrees

slides.narration: In a pure coil, the supply voltage must at every instant equal L times the rate of change of current. Integrating a sine gives a negative cosine, so the current is a sine wave shifted back by a quarter of a cycle: it lags the voltage by ninety degrees. Its peak is V nought over omega L, so the inductive reactance is omega L, which grows in proportion to the frequency.

slides.heading: Pure capacitor: the current leads by 90°
slides.body_md:
The charge follows the voltage, $q = Cv = CV_0\sin\omega t$, so
$$i = \dfrac{dq}{dt} = \omega CV_0\cos\omega t = I_0\sin\left(\omega t + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right), \qquad I_0 = \dfrac{V_0}{1/\omega C}$$
So $i$ **leads** $v$ by $\pi/2$, and the **capacitive reactance** is $X_C = \dfrac{1}{\omega C} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi fC}$.
bullets: $X_C \propto 1/f$: a capacitor passes high frequencies easily; for DC ($f = 0$) $X_C$ is infinite, so it **blocks** a steady current.

points.label: i peaks a quarter cycle earlier (at 0° and 360°)

visual.alt: Voltage across a pure capacitor and the current in it over one cycle: the current reaches each peak a quarter of a cycle before the voltage, so it leads by 90 degrees

slides.narration: For a capacitor, the charge on the plates follows the voltage. The current is the rate of change of that charge, and the rate of change of a sine is a cosine, so the current reaches its peak a quarter of a cycle before the voltage: it leads by ninety degrees. Its size is omega C times the voltage, so the capacitive reactance is one over omega C, which falls as the frequency rises.

slides.heading: Reactance against frequency
slides.body_md: For the coil and the capacitor of worked example 2:
bullets: $X_L = 2\pi fL$: a **straight line through the origin**.
$X_C = 1/(2\pi fC)$: a curve falling as $1/f$ (a **rectangular hyperbola**), very large at low $f$.
At high frequency a coil behaves almost like a break in the circuit, a capacitor almost like a plain wire; at low frequency the reverse.

visual.alt: Reactance against frequency for the coil and capacitor of worked example 2: the inductive reactance is a straight line through the origin, the capacitive reactance a curve falling as one over f; they are equal at about 69 hertz
visual.caption: X_L ∝ f; X_C ∝ 1/f.

slides.narration: Plot both reactances against frequency. The coil gives a straight line through the origin: double the frequency and you double its opposition. The capacitor gives a curve that falls as one over f: huge at low frequency, small at high frequency. So at high frequencies a coil nearly stops the current while a capacitor lets it through, and at low frequencies it is the other way round.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a coil and a capacitor on the mains
slides.body_md: A coil of inductance 0.35 H and a 15 μF capacitor (both ideal) are connected in turn to 230 V, 50 Hz mains. Find the reactance of each and the rms current it draws. What are the reactances at 200 Hz?
bullets: $X_L = 2\pi \times 50 \times 0.35 \approx 110.0$ Ω, so $I = \dfrac{230}{110.0} \approx 2.09$ A (lagging by 90°).
$X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi \times 50 \times 15 \times 10^{-6}} \approx 212.2$ Ω, so $I = \dfrac{230}{212.2} \approx 1.08$ A (leading by 90°).
At 200 Hz (four times the frequency): $X_L \approx 440$ Ω and $X_C \approx 53.1$ Ω.

visual.alt: Reactance against frequency for the coil and capacitor of worked example 2: the inductive reactance is a straight line through the origin, the capacitive reactance a curve falling as one over f; they are equal at about 69 hertz
visual.caption: X_L ∝ f; X_C ∝ 1/f.

slides.narration: At fifty hertz the coil’s reactance is two pi times fifty times nought point three five, about a hundred and ten ohms, so it draws about two point one amperes. The capacitor’s reactance is about two hundred and twelve ohms, so it draws about one point one amperes. At four times the frequency the coil’s reactance is four times larger, about four hundred and forty ohms, and the capacitor’s is a quarter, about fifty three ohms.

slides.body_md: R, L and C in series carry the **same current** $i = I_0\sin\omega t$. Take $I$ as the reference phasor:
bullets: $V_R = IR$ is **in phase** with $I$; $V_L = IX_L$ **leads** $I$ by 90°; $V_C = IX_C$ **lags** $I$ by 90°.
The voltmeter readings $V_R$, $V_L$, $V_C$ do **not** add up to the supply voltage: they must be added **as phasors**.

slides.narration: Now join a resistor, a coil and a capacitor in series. The same current flows through all three, so we take it as the reference. The voltage across the resistor is in step with the current, the voltage across the coil is a quarter cycle ahead, and the voltage across the capacitor is a quarter cycle behind. That is why the three voltmeter readings add up to more than the supply voltage.

slides.heading: Impedance and phase angle by phasors
slides.body_md:
$V_L$ and $V_C$ point in opposite directions, so they combine to $V_L - V_C$, at right angles to $V_R$. The supply voltage is the resultant:
$$V^2 = V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2 = I^2\left[R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2\right]$$
$$Z = \dfrac{V}{I} = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}, \qquad \tan\phi = \dfrac{X_L - X_C}{R}$$
bullets: $X_L > X_C$: **inductive**, current lags $V$ by $\phi$. $X_C > X_L$: **capacitive**, current leads. $Z$ is the **impedance** (ohm).

slides.narration: On the phasor diagram the coil’s voltage points up and the capacitor’s points down, so they partly cancel, leaving V L minus V C at right angles to the resistor’s voltage. Pythagoras then gives the supply voltage, and dividing by the current gives the impedance: root of R squared plus the square of the net reactance. The angle between the supply voltage and the current is the phase angle phi.

slides.heading: Special cases: RL and RC circuits
slides.body_md: Drop one element from the series circuit:
columns:
**R and L in series**
- $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + \omega^2L^2}$
- $\tan\phi = \omega L/R$
- current **lags** the voltage by an angle between 0° and 90°
- e.g. a real coil, which has some resistance

**R and C in series**
- $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + 1/\omega^2C^2}$
- $\tan\phi = 1/\omega CR$
- current **leads** the voltage by an angle between 0° and 90°
- the phasor $V_C$ points down, so $V$ lies below $V_R$

rows: L, C and R in series
lags if $X_L > X_C$, leads if $X_C > X_L$

visual.alt: Table of the impedance, phase angle and phase of the current for RL, RC and LCR series circuits

slides.narration: Two special cases are common. A resistor with a coil, which is just what a real coil is, has impedance root of R squared plus omega L squared, and the current lags by an angle whose tangent is omega L over R. A resistor with a capacitor has impedance root of R squared plus one over omega C all squared, and the current leads by an angle whose tangent is one over omega C R.

slides.heading: Impedance and current against frequency
slides.body_md: For a fixed L, C and R, sweep the supply frequency:
bullets: Low $f$: $X_C$ is large, so $Z$ is large and the circuit is **capacitive**.
At one frequency $f_0$, $X_L = X_C$: $Z$ is **least**, equal to $R$, and the current $I = V/Z$ is **greatest**.
High $f$: $X_L$ is large, so $Z$ rises again and the circuit is **inductive**. (More on $f_0$ in Part 2.)

functions.label: Z, with L = 25 mH, C = 4.0 μF, R = 10 Ω

visual.alt: Impedance of a series LCR circuit against frequency: large at low frequency where the capacitor dominates, falling to a minimum equal to R at the resonant frequency of about 503 hertz, and rising again at high frequency where the inductor dominates
visual.caption: I = V/Z is greatest where Z is least.

slides.narration: If we sweep the frequency of the supply, the impedance changes. At low frequencies the capacitor’s reactance dominates and the impedance is large. At high frequencies the coil’s reactance dominates. In between there is one frequency where the two reactances are equal and cancel: there the impedance falls to just R, and the current, V over Z, rises to its largest value.

slides.narration: To sum up: an alternating current is described by its peak, frequency and phase. Its half cycle mean is two over pi of the peak and its rms value one over root two of the peak. Current is in phase with the voltage in a resistor, lags in a coil and leads in a capacitor. In a series circuit the voltages add as phasors, giving the impedance and the phase angle.

slides.narration: In this part we ask how much power an alternating current circuit actually uses, and why some current does no work at all. We see how a choke controls a current without wasting energy, how a series circuit responds strongly at one frequency, how energy swings to and fro in a coil and capacitor, and finally how a generator produces the alternating emf in the first place.

slides.heading: Average power in an AC circuit
slides.body_md:
With $v = V_0\sin\omega t$ and $i = I_0\sin(\omega t - \phi)$, the instantaneous power is
$$p = vi = V_0I_0\sin\omega t\sin(\omega t - \phi) = \dfrac{V_0I_0}{2}\left[\cos\phi - \cos(2\omega t - \phi)\right]$$
The second term averages to zero over a cycle, so
$$P = \dfrac{V_0I_0}{2}\cos\phi = V_\text{rms}I_\text{rms}\cos\phi$$
bullets: $V_\text{rms}I_\text{rms}$ is the **apparent power** (volt-ampere, VA); $P$ is the true (average) power, in watts.

y.label: fraction of V₀, I₀ or V₀I₀

visual.alt: Voltage, current and instantaneous power over one cycle when the current lags by 60 degrees: the power curve swings at twice the supply frequency and is negative for part of each half cycle, when energy flows back to the supply; its average is a quarter of V nought I nought
visual.caption: p = vi; the average is V_rms I_rms cos φ.

slides.narration: The power at any instant is the voltage times the current. Using a product to sum formula, it splits into a steady part, half V nought I nought cos phi, and a part that oscillates at twice the supply frequency. The oscillating part averages to zero over a cycle, so the average power is V rms times I rms times cos phi. The product of the rms values alone is called the apparent power.

slides.heading: Power factor
slides.body_md:
The factor $\cos\phi$ is the **power factor**. For a series LCR circuit
$$\cos\phi = \dfrac{R}{Z} = \dfrac{P}{V_\text{rms}I_\text{rms}}, \qquad P = I_\text{rms}^2R$$
bullets: Pure resistor: $\cos\phi = 1$. Pure inductor or capacitor: $\cos\phi = 0$, so **no average power**: energy taken in one quarter cycle is returned in the next.
Only the resistance turns electrical energy into heat or work.

slides.narration: Cos phi is called the power factor. For a series circuit it equals R over Z, so the average power is just the rms current squared times the resistance. A pure resistor has a power factor of one. A pure coil or capacitor has a power factor of zero: it stores energy for a quarter cycle and hands it back in the next, so over a whole cycle it takes no power.

slides.heading: Active and wattless current
slides.body_md: Resolve the current phasor along and across the voltage:
bullets: $I\cos\phi$, **in phase** with $V$: the **active** component, which carries all the power $P = V(I\cos\phi)$.
$I\sin\phi$, **in quadrature** (90°) with $V$: the **wattless current**, which does no work over a cycle.
A wattless current still flows in the cables and heats them ($I^2R$ losses), so supply companies want a power factor close to 1.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a pump motor
slides.body_md: A water-pump motor draws 4.0 A (rms) from 230 V mains at a power factor of 0.80, lagging. Find the apparent power, the average power, the phase angle, and the active and wattless components of the current.
bullets: Apparent power $= 230 \times 4.0 = 920$ VA; $P = 920 \times 0.80 = 736$ W.
$\phi = \cos^{-1} 0.80 \approx 36.9^\circ$, so $\sin\phi = 0.60$.
Active current $= 4.0 \times 0.80 = 3.2$ A; wattless current $= 4.0 \times 0.60 = 2.4$ A. Check: $\sqrt{3.2^2 + 2.4^2} = 4.0$ A.

slides.heading: The choke coil
slides.body_md: A **choke** is a coil of large inductance and very small resistance, wound on a laminated iron core. In series with a load it reduces an alternating current:
bullets: Its power factor $R/Z$ is almost zero, so it takes **almost no power**; the current through it is nearly all wattless.
A resistor would reduce the current equally well but turn the extra energy into **heat**.
Used in the fittings of fluorescent tubes and in arc lamps; it cannot control DC, for which $X_L = 0$.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: running a lamp from the mains

bullets: (a) The resistor drops $230 - 100 = 130$ V: $R = \dfrac{130}{4.0} = 32.5$ Ω, wasting $4.0^2 \times 32.5 = 520$ W.

With a choke, the lamp’s twenty five ohms and the choke’s reactance must give an impedance of fifty seven and a half ohms, so the reactance is about fifty one point eight ohms and the inductance about nought point one six five henry.

slides.heading: Electrical resonance
slides.body_md:
The current in a series LCR circuit is greatest when $X_L = X_C$, i.e. $\omega L = \dfrac{1}{\omega C}$:
$$\omega_0 = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}, \qquad f_0 = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$$
bullets: At resonance $Z = R$ (least), $I_0 = V/R$ (greatest), $\phi = 0$ and the power factor is 1.
$V_L$ and $V_C$ are equal and opposite; each can be **many times** the supply voltage.
$f_0$ does not depend on $R$; $R$ decides the height and sharpness of the peak.

visual.alt: Resonance curves, rms current against frequency for the circuit of worked example 6 with R equal to 10 ohms and with R equal to 30 ohms: both peak at the same resonant frequency, about 503 hertz, but the curve for the smaller resistance is higher and much sharper; its half-power frequencies f1 and f2 are marked
visual.caption: Bandwidth f₂ − f₁ = R/(2πL); smaller R gives a sharper peak.

slides.narration: At one particular frequency the coil’s reactance exactly equals the capacitor’s, and they cancel. This is resonance. The impedance falls to R, the current is as large as it can be, and the current is in phase with the supply. The resonant frequency is one over two pi root L C, whatever the resistance. A smaller resistance gives a taller, sharper peak.

slides.heading: Bandwidth and Q factor
slides.body_md:
The **half-power frequencies** $f_1$ and $f_2$ are where $I = I_0/\sqrt2$ (power half its peak). For a series LCR circuit (formulae only; derivations are not required):
$$\Delta\omega = \omega_2 - \omega_1 = \dfrac{R}{L}, \qquad Q = \dfrac{\omega_0}{\Delta\omega} = \dfrac{\omega_0L}{R} = \dfrac{1}{R}\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{C}}$$
bullets: $\Delta f = f_2 - f_1 = \dfrac{R}{2\pi L}$ is the **bandwidth**; the **quality factor** $Q$ measures the sharpness of the resonance.
At resonance $V_L = V_C = QV$: $Q$ is also the voltage magnification.
A radio tuner needs a large $Q$ (small $R$) to pick out one station.

visual.alt: Resonance curves, rms current against frequency for the circuit of worked example 6 with R equal to 10 ohms and with R equal to 30 ohms: both peak at the same resonant frequency, about 503 hertz, but the curve for the smaller resistance is higher and much sharper; its half-power frequencies f1 and f2 are marked
visual.caption: Bandwidth f₂ − f₁ = R/(2πL); smaller R gives a sharper peak.

slides.narration: How sharp is the peak? Find the two frequencies where the current has fallen to one over root two of its peak, so the power has halved. The gap between them is the bandwidth: R over L in angular frequency, or R over two pi L in hertz. The quality factor Q is the resonant frequency divided by the bandwidth. A small resistance means a narrow band and a large Q.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: a resonant circuit
slides.body_md: A series circuit has $L = 25$ mH, $C = 4.0$ μF and $R = 10$ Ω, with a 5.0 V rms variable-frequency supply. Find $f_0$, the current and $V_L$ at resonance, the Q factor and the bandwidth.
bullets: $\omega_0 = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{0.025 \times 4.0 \times 10^{-6}}} \approx 3162$ rad s$^{-1}$, $f_0 = \dfrac{\omega_0}{2\pi} \approx 503$ Hz.
$I_0 = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{5.0}{10} = 0.50$ A; $X_L = \omega_0L \approx 79.1$ Ω, so $V_L = V_C \approx 39.5$ V, about eight times the supply.
$Q = \dfrac{\omega_0L}{R} \approx 7.91$; $\Delta f = \dfrac{R}{2\pi L} = \dfrac{10}{2\pi \times 0.025} \approx 63.7$ Hz.

visual.alt: Resonance curves, rms current against frequency for the circuit of worked example 6 with R equal to 10 ohms and with R equal to 30 ohms: both peak at the same resonant frequency, about 503 hertz, but the curve for the smaller resistance is higher and much sharper; its half-power frequencies f1 and f2 are marked
visual.caption: Bandwidth f₂ − f₁ = R/(2πL); smaller R gives a sharper peak.

slides.narration: The resonant angular frequency is one over the root of L C, about three thousand one hundred and sixty radians per second, so the resonant frequency is about five hundred and three hertz. The current is five volts over ten ohms, half an ampere. The coil’s reactance there is about seventy nine ohms, so nearly forty volts appears across it. slides.heading: The AC generator: principle and construction
slides.body_md: **Principle:** electromagnetic induction. A coil turned in a magnetic field has a changing flux through it, so an emf is induced.
bullets: **Armature:** a coil of many turns on a soft-iron core, turned by a turbine or engine.
**Field magnet:** strong poles giving a uniform radial or uniform field.
**Slip rings:** two rings fixed to the axle, one joined to each end of the coil; they turn with it.
**Brushes:** carbon blocks pressing on the rings, connecting the turning coil to the external circuit.

slides.heading: Theory: the sinusoidal emf
slides.body_md:
A coil of $N$ turns and area $A$ turns at angular speed $\omega$ in a uniform field $B$. If its normal is along $B$ at $t = 0$, the angle at time $t$ is $\theta = \omega t$ and
$$\Phi = NBA\cos\omega t, \qquad e = -\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} = NBA\omega\sin\omega t = e_0\sin\omega t$$
bullets: Peak emf $e_0 = NBA\omega$, when the plane of the coil is **along** $B$ (flux zero but changing fastest).
$e = 0$ when the plane is **perpendicular** to $B$ (flux greatest).
Frequency of the AC = number of rotations per second; the emf reverses every half turn.

slides.body_md: A rectangular coil of 150 turns, 20 cm × 12 cm, turns at 50 revolutions per second about an axis perpendicular to a uniform field of 0.30 T. Find the peak and rms emf and the frequency.

$e_0 = NBA\omega = 150 \times 0.30 \times 0.024 \times 314.2 \approx 339$ V.
$e_\text{rms} = \dfrac{e_0}{\sqrt2} \approx 240$ V; frequency 50 Hz (one cycle per turn).

slides.heading: AC and DC compared
slides.body_md: How the two kinds of current differ:
columns:
**Alternating current**
- Reverses direction periodically (50 Hz in India); value varies
- Voltage easily changed by transformers, so power is sent over long distances at high voltage with small loss
- Measured by its rms value

**Direct current**
- Flows in one direction, usually steady
- Needed for charging batteries, electroplating and electronic circuits
- Cannot be stepped up or down by a transformer
- Measured by moving-coil meters

rows: easily stepped up or down by transformers
cells, batteries, solar cells, DC dynamos
transmission over long distances, motors, heaters

slides.narration: Alternating current reverses direction many times a second, and its voltage is easily raised or lowered by transformers, so it can be sent long distances at high voltage with little loss. Direct current flows one way only. It cannot be transformed, but it is essential for charging batteries, for electroplating and inside electronic devices, which convert the mains to direct current.

sections.heading: 1. Sinusoidal AC; mean and rms values
sections.body_md:
- $i = I_0\sin(\omega t + \phi_0)$: **peak** $I_0$, **period** $T$, **frequency** $f = 1/T$, angular frequency $\omega = 2\pi f$, **phase** $(\omega t + \phi_0)$. Indian mains: 230 V rms, 50 Hz, $T = 20$ ms.
- A **phasor** is a vector of length equal to the peak, turning anticlockwise at $\omega$; its projection gives the instantaneous value. The quantity whose phasor is ahead **leads**.
- **Mean over a half cycle:** $\bar I = \dfrac{2}{T}\int_0^{T/2} I_0\sin\omega t\,dt = \dfrac{2I_0}{\pi} \approx 0.637\,I_0$. Over a full cycle the mean is zero.
- **rms value:** the steady current giving the same heating in a resistor. $\overline{\sin^2\omega t} = \tfrac12$, so $I_\text{rms} = I_0/\sqrt2 \approx 0.707\,I_0$ (sine waves only). AC meters and ratings use rms values.

key_terms.definition_md: The steady (DC) value that would produce the same heat in a given resistor in the same time; I₀/√2 for a sinusoidal current.
A rotating vector whose length is the peak value of a sinusoidal quantity and whose projection gives its instantaneous value.

sections.heading: 2. AC through pure R, L and C
sections.body_md:
- **Resistor:** $i$ in phase with $v$; $I_\text{rms} = V_\text{rms}/R$.
- **Inductor:** $v = L\,di/dt$ gives $i = I_0\sin(\omega t - \pi/2)$: current **lags** by 90°. **Inductive reactance** $X_L = \omega L = 2\pi fL$.
- **Capacitor:** $i = dq/dt = C\,dv/dt$ gives $i = I_0\sin(\omega t + \pi/2)$: current **leads** by 90°. **Capacitive reactance** $X_C = 1/(\omega C) = 1/(2\pi fC)$.
- Graphs against f: $X_L$ a straight line through the origin; $X_C$ a rectangular hyperbola. A coil passes DC and low frequencies; a capacitor blocks DC and passes high frequencies.

key_terms.definition_md: The opposition of an inductor (ωL) or a capacitor (1/ωC) to alternating current, in ohms; it depends on frequency and causes no heating.

sections.heading: 3. The series LCR circuit
sections.body_md:
- Same current through all; phasors: $V_R$ along $I$, $V_L$ 90° ahead, $V_C$ 90° behind. Add as phasors: $V^2 = V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2$.
- **Impedance** $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$, $I = V/Z$; **phase angle** $\tan\phi = (X_L - X_C)/R$. $X_L > X_C$: inductive, $I$ lags; $X_C > X_L$: capacitive, $I$ leads.
- **RL:** $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + \omega^2L^2}$, $\tan\phi = \omega L/R$ (lags). **RC:** $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + 1/\omega^2C^2}$, $\tan\phi = 1/\omega CR$ (leads).
- Against frequency: $Z$ falls to a minimum $R$ where $X_L = X_C$ and rises again; $I = V/Z$ peaks there. The voltage across L or C can exceed the supply voltage.

key_terms.definition_md: The total opposition of a circuit to AC, Z = V/I; for a series LCR circuit √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²).
The angle φ by which the supply voltage leads (or lags) the current; tan φ = (X_L − X_C)/R.

sections.heading: 4. Power, power factor, wattless current and the choke
sections.body_md:
- $p = vi$; average over a cycle: $P = V_\text{rms}I_\text{rms}\cos\phi = I_\text{rms}^2R$. $V_\text{rms}I_\text{rms}$ is the apparent power (VA).
- **Power factor** $\cos\phi = R/Z$: 1 for a pure resistor (and at resonance), 0 for a pure L or C.
- **Wattless current:** the component $I\sin\phi$ in quadrature with $V$; it does no work over a cycle but still heats the supply cables. The active component is $I\cos\phi$.
- **Choke coil:** large L, very small R, laminated iron core; power factor nearly zero, so it limits an AC with almost no loss (a resistor would waste $I^2R$).

key_terms.definition_md: cos φ, the ratio of the true power to the apparent power V_rms I_rms; equal to R/Z for a series circuit.
The component I sin φ of an alternating current that is 90° out of phase with the voltage and so delivers no average power.
An inductor of large inductance and negligible resistance used to limit an alternating current without wasting energy.

sections.heading: 5. Resonance, bandwidth, Q factor and LC oscillations
sections.body_md:
- **Resonance** when $X_L = X_C$: $\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC}$, $f_0 = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$. Then $Z = R$, $I_0 = V/R$, $\phi = 0$, power factor 1; $V_L = V_C$, each possibly much larger than $V$.
- **Half-power frequencies** $f_1$, $f_2$: $I = I_0/\sqrt2$. **Bandwidth** $\Delta\omega = R/L$ ($\Delta f = R/2\pi L$). **Q factor** $Q = \omega_0/\Delta\omega = \omega_0L/R = \tfrac1R\sqrt{L/C}$; $V_L = QV$ at resonance. (Formulae only; derivations not required.)
- Smaller R: taller, sharper peak, larger Q, same $f_0$. Used in radio tuning.
- **LC oscillations** (qualitative): a charged capacitor across a coil; energy passes back and forth between the electric field of C and the magnetic field of L at $f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$; resistance makes the oscillations die away.

key_terms.definition_md: The frequency 1/(2π√(LC)) at which X_L = X_C in a series LCR circuit, so that the impedance is least and the current greatest.
ω₀/Δω = ω₀L/R for a series LCR circuit: a measure of the sharpness of resonance.
The gap between the two half-power frequencies, at which the current is I₀/√2.

sections.heading: 6. The AC generator; AC and DC
sections.body_md:
- **Principle:** electromagnetic induction in a coil turned in a magnetic field. **Parts:** armature coil, field magnet, slip rings, carbon brushes; driven by a turbine or engine.
- **Theory:** with the normal along B at $t = 0$, $\Phi = NBA\cos\omega t$ and $e = -d\Phi/dt = NBA\omega\sin\omega t$; peak $e_0 = NBA\omega$ when the plane is along B; $e = 0$ when the plane faces B. Frequency = rotations per second.
- **AC against DC:** AC reverses periodically and is easily transformed for efficient long-distance transmission; DC flows one way and is needed for charging, electroplating and electronics. AC is measured by its rms value.

questions.stem_md: Two voltages displayed on a double-beam oscilloscope are $v_1 = 12\sin(200\pi t)$ and $v_2 = 12\cos(200\pi t)$, in volts, with $t$ in seconds. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: $v_2$ leads $v_1$ by a quarter of a period, 2.5 ms
$v_1$ leads $v_2$ by a quarter of a period, 2.5 ms
$v_2$ leads $v_1$ by half a period, 5.0 ms
they are in phase, because their peak values are equal

questions.solution_md: $\omega = 200\pi$ rad s$^{-1}$, so $f = 100$ Hz and $T = 10$ ms. Since $\cos\theta = \sin(\theta + \pi/2)$, $v_2$ is $v_1$ shifted ahead by $\pi/2$, a quarter of a period: $T/4 = 2.5$ ms — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A moving-coil ammeter (meant for DC) and a hot-wire ammeter are joined in series in a 50 Hz circuit carrying a sinusoidal current of peak value 2.0 A. Their readings are

options.text_md: about 1.4 A on both
zero and about 1.4 A
about 1.3 A and 2.0 A
zero and 2.0 A

questions.solution_md: The moving-coil meter responds to the average current, which is zero over each cycle (its needle cannot follow 50 Hz). The hot-wire meter responds to the heating, i.e. to the mean of $i^2$, so it reads the rms value $2.0/\sqrt2 \approx 1.4$ A — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A signal generator gives a square-wave voltage that switches between +6.0 V and −6.0 V, spending equal times at each value. Its rms value is

options.text_md: zero

questions.solution_md: At every instant $v^2 = 36$ V², so the mean of $v^2$ is 36 V² and $V_\text{rms} = 6.0$ V. The rule $V_0/\sqrt2$ (which would give 4.2 V) holds only for sinusoidal waves — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The emf of a source is $e = 170\sin(120\pi t)$ volts. Starting from $t = 0$, how long does the emf take to rise to 85 V for the first time? Give the answer in ms (3 significant figures).
A sinusoidal current has an rms value of 3.0 A. Find its mean value over a half cycle, in amperes (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $I_0 = \sqrt2\,I_\text{rms}$ and $\bar I = \dfrac{2I_0}{\pi} = \dfrac{2\sqrt2}{\pi}I_\text{rms}$, so $\bar I = 0.9003 \times 3.0 = 2.70$ A.

questions.stem_md: An immersion heater rod of resistance 46 Ω is connected to 230 V, 50 Hz mains. Find the peak value of the current through it, in amperes (3 significant figures).

**Assertion (A):** Over one complete cycle, the average value of a sinusoidal alternating current is zero.

**Reason (R):** The heat produced by an alternating current in a resistor is proportional to the square of the current.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, but R does not explain A: the full-cycle mean is zero because the negative half cycle exactly mirrors the positive one; R is about heating, which is why the rms value is used — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The relation $I_\text{rms} = I_0/\sqrt2$ holds for every alternating current, whatever the shape of its waveform.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. It holds only for sinusoidal currents. A square wave of peak $I_0$, for example, has $I_\text{rms} = I_0$, because $i^2 = I_0^2$ at every instant.

questions.stem_md: Indian household mains completes 50 cycles every second, reversing its direction 100 times; so each complete cycle of the mains voltage lasts ___ ms.
Why is the mean value of an alternating current quoted over a half cycle rather than over a full cycle? Calculate the half-cycle mean of a sinusoidal current whose rms value is 5.0 A.

answer.model_answer_md: Over a full cycle the positive and negative halves cancel, so the mean is always zero and tells us nothing; over a **half cycle** it is $2I_0/\pi$, which measures, for example, the charge sent in one half cycle. Here $I_0 = \sqrt2 \times 5.0 \approx 7.07$ A, so $\bar I = \dfrac{2 \times 7.07}{\pi} \approx 4.50$ A.

questions.solution_md: Full-cycle mean zero; 2I₀/π.

marking_scheme.step: Full-cycle mean is zero; half-cycle mean 2I₀/π

questions.stem_md: Define the rms value of an alternating current. Derive the relation between the rms value and the peak value of a sinusoidal current $i = I_0\sin\omega t$. Hence find the peak voltage of 230 V mains.

answer.model_answer_md: The **rms value** is the steady current that would produce the same heat in a given resistor in the same time. Heat in time $T$ is $\int_0^T i^2R\,dt$, so $I_\text{rms}^2 = \overline{i^2} = \dfrac{1}{T}\int_0^T I_0^2\sin^2\omega t\,dt = \dfrac{I_0^2}{T}\int_0^T \dfrac{1 - \cos 2\omega t}{2}\,dt = \dfrac{I_0^2}{2}$, since $\cos 2\omega t$ averages to zero over a cycle. Hence $I_\text{rms} = \dfrac{I_0}{\sqrt2}$. For the mains $V_0 = \sqrt2 \times 230 \approx 325$ V.

questions.solution_md: Mean of sin² over a cycle is 1/2.

marking_scheme.step: Mean of i² = I₀²/2, so I_rms = I₀/√2

questions.stem_md: A capacitor has a reactance of 90 Ω on a 50 Hz supply. When it is connected instead to a 150 Hz supply, its reactance becomes

options.text_md: 90 Ω, since reactance does not depend on frequency

questions.solution_md: $X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi fC} \propto \dfrac{1}{f}$. Tripling the frequency divides the reactance by 3: $90/3 = 30$ Ω — option (c).

questions.stem_md: An ideal capacitor is connected across a sinusoidal supply. At the instant the voltage across it reaches its positive peak, the current in the circuit is

options.text_md: at its positive peak, in step with the voltage
zero, and about to reverse as the capacitor starts to discharge
at its negative peak
half its peak value

questions.solution_md: $i = C\,\dfrac{dv}{dt}$. At the peak of $v$ the slope is zero, so $i = 0$; just afterwards $v$ falls, so $i$ becomes negative and the capacitor discharges. This is the 90° lead of the current — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A coil of inductance 80 mH and negligible resistance is connected to 230 V, 50 Hz mains. Find the rms current it draws, in amperes (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $X_L = 2\pi fL = 2\pi \times 50 \times 0.080 \approx 25.13$ Ω; $I = \dfrac{V}{X_L} = \dfrac{230}{25.13} = 9.15$ A.

questions.stem_md: What capacitance has a reactance of 400 Ω at 50 Hz? Give the answer in μF (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi fX_C} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi \times 50 \times 400} \approx 7.96 \times 10^{-6}$ F, i.e. $7.96 \times 10^{-6} \times 10^{6} = 7.96$ μF.

questions.stem_md: A capacitor draws 0.60 A from a 230 V, 50 Hz supply. On board a ship it is connected to a 230 V, 60 Hz supply instead. What current does it draw now, in amperes?
questions.solution_md: $I = \dfrac{V}{X_C} = 2\pi fCV \propto f$ at fixed voltage, so $I = 0.60 \times \dfrac{60}{50} = 0.72$ A.

questions.stem_md: A loudspeaker crossover network uses a 50 mH coil. What capacitance has the same reactance as this coil at 1.0 kHz? Give the answer in μF (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $\omega L = \dfrac{1}{\omega C}$ gives $C = \dfrac{1}{\omega^2L} = \dfrac{1}{(2\pi \times 1000)^2 \times 0.050} \approx 5.07 \times 10^{-7}$ F, i.e. $5.07 \times 10^{-7} \times 10^{6} = 0.507$ μF.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In a circuit containing only an ideal inductor, the current reaches its maximum a quarter of a cycle after the applied voltage does.

**Reason (R):** The emf induced in the inductor opposes every change of the current through it.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R explains A: because the self-induced emf opposes changes of current, the current builds up only while the voltage acts, reaching its peak when the voltage has fallen to zero — a lag of 90° — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A lamp in series with a large capacitor glows on 230 V AC mains but stays dark on a 230 V DC supply.

**Reason (R):** The reactance of a capacitor, $1/(\omega C)$, becomes infinitely large when $\omega = 0$.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R explains A: a steady supply has zero frequency, so the capacitor offers infinite opposition once it has charged, and no current flows; on AC it charges and discharges continually — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? At very high frequencies an inductor behaves almost like a plain connecting wire, while a capacitor behaves almost like an open switch.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. It is the other way round: $X_L = 2\pi fL$ becomes very large (the coil nearly blocks the current), while $X_C = 1/(2\pi fC)$ becomes very small (the capacitor passes it easily).

questions.stem_md: For a capacitor on an AC supply, the ratio of the rms voltage across it to the rms current through it, equal to 1/(ωC), is called its capacitive ___.
questions.solution_md: Its capacitive **reactance**, measured in ohms.

questions.stem_md: Match each graph drawn against the supply frequency f (Column A) with the circuit quantity it describes (Column B).

options.text_md: A straight line through the origin, rising with f
A curve falling as 1/f, very large at low f
A horizontal line, the same at every f
A curve with a minimum at one frequency

match_right.text_md: impedance of a series LCR circuit

questions.solution_md: Straight line through the origin → X_L = 2πfL (1 → r); falling as 1/f → X_C = 1/(2πfC) (2 → p); horizontal → R, independent of f (3 → s); minimum at one frequency → Z, least (= R) at resonance (4 → q).

questions.stem_md: In a hi-fi speaker box, the tweeter (for high notes) is fed through a capacitor and the woofer (for low notes) through an inductor. Explain how this sends each range of frequencies to the right speaker.

answer.model_answer_md: The capacitor’s reactance $X_C = 1/(2\pi fC)$ is **small at high frequency** and large at low frequency, so it passes high notes to the tweeter and blocks low ones. The inductor’s reactance $X_L = 2\pi fL$ is **small at low frequency** and large at high frequency, so it passes low notes to the woofer and chokes high ones.

questions.solution_md: X_C falls with f; X_L rises with f.

marking_scheme.step: Capacitor: small X_C at high f, passes high notes to the tweeter
Inductor: small X_L at low f, passes low notes to the woofer

questions.stem_md: A capacitor of capacitance C is connected across a source of emf $e = E_0\sin\omega t$. Obtain an expression for the current in the circuit and show that it leads the emf by π/2. Write the capacitive reactance and state how it varies with frequency.

answer.model_answer_md: The charge on the capacitor follows the emf: $q = Ce = CE_0\sin\omega t$. The current is $i = \dfrac{dq}{dt} = \omega CE_0\cos\omega t = I_0\sin\left(\omega t + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, with $I_0 = \omega CE_0 = \dfrac{E_0}{1/\omega C}$. So the current reaches each peak a quarter of a cycle **before** the emf: it **leads** by π/2. The capacitive reactance is $X_C = \dfrac{1}{\omega C} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi fC}$, inversely proportional to the frequency (infinite for DC).

questions.solution_md: i = dq/dt = C de/dt.

marking_scheme.step: q = CE₀ sin ωt and i = ωCE₀ cos ωt
cos ωt = sin(ωt + π/2): leads by π/2

questions.stem_md: A series AC circuit has R = 40 Ω, X_L = 25 Ω and X_C = 55 Ω. The current in it

options.text_md: lags behind the supply voltage by about 37°
leads the supply voltage by about 53°
is in phase with the supply voltage
leads the supply voltage by about 37°

questions.solution_md: $\tan\phi = \dfrac{X_L - X_C}{R} = \dfrac{25 - 55}{40} = -0.75$, so $|\phi| \approx 36.9^\circ$. Since $X_C > X_L$ the circuit is capacitive and the current leads — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The frequency of the supply to a series LCR circuit is raised steadily from well below its resonant frequency to well above it. The impedance of the circuit

options.text_md: falls to a least value equal to R and then rises again
rises steadily, because X_L increases with frequency
falls steadily, because X_C decreases with frequency
stays equal to R throughout

questions.solution_md: $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$. Below $f_0$, $X_C$ dominates and $Z$ is large; at $f_0$, $X_L = X_C$ and $Z = R$; above $f_0$, $X_L$ dominates and $Z$ rises — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In a series RC circuit on an AC supply, ideal voltmeters read 12 V across the resistor and 16 V across the capacitor. The supply voltage and the phase of the current are

options.text_md: 28 V, with the current leading by 90°
20 V, with the current lagging by about 53°
20 V, with the current leading by about 53°
4 V, with the current in phase

questions.solution_md: $V_R$ and $V_C$ are at right angles: $V = \sqrt{12^2 + 16^2} = 20$ V. $\tan\phi = \dfrac{16}{12}$ gives $\phi \approx 53.1^\circ$, and in an RC circuit the current leads — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A coil of resistance 15 Ω and inductance 64 mH is connected to 230 V, 50 Hz mains. Find the rms current, in amperes (3 significant figures).
A 120 Ω resistor is joined in series with a 15 μF capacitor across a 50 Hz supply. Find the phase angle between the current and the supply voltage, in degrees (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi \times 50 \times 15 \times 10^{-6}} \approx 212.2$ Ω; $\tan\phi = \dfrac{X_C}{R} = \dfrac{212.2}{120} \approx 1.768$, so $\phi = 60.5$°, the current leading.

questions.stem_md: In a series LCR circuit on an AC supply, ideal voltmeters read 60 V across the resistor, 140 V across the inductor and 60 V across the capacitor. Find the rms supply voltage, in volts.
questions.solution_md: $V = \sqrt{V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2} = \sqrt{60^2 + (140 - 60)^2} = \sqrt{3600 + 6400} = 100$ V (not the arithmetic sum, 260 V).

questions.stem_md: A coil connected to a 12 V DC supply draws 2.0 A. Connected instead to a 12 V (rms), 50 Hz supply, it draws 1.2 A. Find (a) its resistance, (b) its impedance and inductance on AC, (c) the phase angle between the current and the voltage on AC.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) On DC there is no reactance: $R = \dfrac{12}{2.0} = 6.0$ Ω.
(b) $Z = \dfrac{12}{1.2} = 10$ Ω, so $X_L = \sqrt{10^2 - 6.0^2} = 8.0$ Ω and $L = \dfrac{X_L}{2\pi f} = \dfrac{8.0}{2\pi \times 50} \approx 0.0255$ H, i.e. about 25.5 mH.
(c) $\tan\phi = \dfrac{X_L}{R} = \dfrac{8.0}{6.0}$, so $\phi \approx 53.1^\circ$, the current lagging.

questions.solution_md: DC gives R; AC gives Z.

marking_scheme.step: R = 6.0 Ω from the DC test

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In a series LCR circuit, the rms voltage across the inductor can be larger than the rms voltage of the supply.

**Reason (R):** The voltages across the inductor and the capacitor are in antiphase, so they partly cancel each other in the phasor sum.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R explains A: since $V_L$ and $V_C$ point in opposite directions on the phasor diagram, only their difference adds to $V_R$, so each of them separately can far exceed the supply voltage (most of all at resonance) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Taking the current as the reference phasor, describe the phasor diagrams of a series RL circuit and of a series RC circuit. In each, state whether the current leads or lags the supply voltage and write tan φ.

answer.model_answer_md: **RL:** $V_R$ along $I$, $V_L$ at 90° **ahead**; the supply voltage lies between them, so the current **lags** by φ with $\tan\phi = \omega L/R$. **RC:** $V_R$ along $I$, $V_C$ at 90° **behind**; the supply voltage lies below $V_R$, so the current **leads** by φ with $\tan\phi = 1/(\omega CR)$.

questions.solution_md: V_L ahead of I, V_C behind I.

marking_scheme.step: RL: V_L 90° ahead of I; current lags; tan φ = ωL/R
RC: V_C 90° behind I; current leads; tan φ = 1/ωCR

questions.stem_md: Using a phasor diagram, derive expressions for the impedance of a series LCR circuit and for the phase angle between the current and the supply voltage. When is such a circuit said to be inductive?

answer.model_answer_md: The same current $I$ flows through R, L and C, so take $I$ as reference. $V_R = IR$ is along $I$, $V_L = IX_L$ is 90° ahead and $V_C = IX_C$ is 90° behind. $V_L$ and $V_C$ are opposite, giving a net $V_L - V_C$ at right angles to $V_R$. The supply voltage is the resultant: $V^2 = V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2 = I^2[R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2]$, so $Z = \dfrac{V}{I} = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$ and $\tan\phi = \dfrac{V_L - V_C}{V_R} = \dfrac{X_L - X_C}{R}$. It is **inductive** when $X_L > X_C$: the voltage then leads the current.

questions.solution_md: Phasor sum of V_R and V_L − V_C.

marking_scheme.step: Phasors: V_R along I, V_L ahead, V_C behind
tan φ = (X_L − X_C)/R; inductive when X_L > X_C

questions.stem_md: A 35 Ω resistor, a 0.18 H inductor and a 120 μF capacitor are joined in series across 230 V, 50 Hz mains. Find (a) the reactances, (b) the impedance and the rms current, (c) the phase angle, saying whether the current leads or lags.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $X_L = 2\pi \times 50 \times 0.18 \approx 56.55$ Ω; $X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi \times 50 \times 120 \times 10^{-6}} \approx 26.53$ Ω.
(b) $Z = \sqrt{35^2 + (56.55 - 26.53)^2} \approx 46.11$ Ω; $I = \dfrac{230}{46.11} \approx 4.99$ A.
(c) $\tan\phi = \dfrac{X_L - X_C}{R} \approx 0.858$, so $\phi \approx 40.6^\circ$; $X_L > X_C$, so the current **lags**.

questions.solution_md: Reactances, then Z = √(R² + (X_L − X_C)²).

questions.stem_md: Describe, as you would sketch them on one set of axes, how the reactance of an inductor, the reactance of a capacitor and the impedance of a series LCR circuit containing both vary with the supply frequency. Mark where the impedance is least, and say how the current behaves there.

answer.model_answer_md: X_L = 2πfL is a **straight line through the origin**. X_C = 1/(2πfC) is a **rectangular hyperbola**, very large at low f and falling towards zero. Z is large at low f (capacitive), falls to a **least value R** at the frequency where the two reactance graphs **cross** (X_L = X_C, the resonant frequency), and rises again at high f (inductive), approaching the X_L line. Since I = V/Z, the current is **greatest** at that crossing and the circuit behaves as a pure resistance there.

questions.solution_md: Line, hyperbola, and a curve with a minimum where they cross.

marking_scheme.step: X_L straight line through origin; X_C hyperbola
Z large at low and high f, least (= R) where X_L = X_C

questions.stem_md: Each of the following loads is connected in turn to the same 230 V, 50 Hz mains. Which one takes the greatest average power?

options.text_md: an ideal inductor of reactance 100 Ω alone
a 100 Ω resistor alone
an ideal capacitor of reactance 100 Ω alone
the 100 Ω resistor in series with an ideal inductor of reactance 100 Ω

questions.solution_md: The ideal inductor and capacitor have power factor 0 and take no average power. The resistor alone takes $\dfrac{230^2}{100} = 529$ W. With the inductor in series, $Z \approx 141$ Ω, so $I \approx 1.63$ A and $P = I^2R \approx 265$ W, only half as much — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A choke coil has a resistance of 1.5 Ω and a reactance of 60 Ω at 50 Hz. Its power factor is closest to
questions.solution_md: $\cos\phi = \dfrac{R}{Z} = \dfrac{1.5}{\sqrt{1.5^2 + 60^2}} \approx \dfrac{1.5}{60.0} \approx 0.025$: almost all of its current is wattless, which is why a choke wastes so little power — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A refrigerator compressor draws 3.2 A (rms) from 230 V mains at a power factor of 0.65. Find the average power it takes, in watts (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $P = V_\text{rms}I_\text{rms}\cos\phi = 230 \times 3.2 \times 0.65 = 478$ W (to 3 significant figures).

questions.stem_md: A series AC circuit has R = 21 Ω, X_L = 32 Ω and X_C = 12 Ω. Find its power factor (3 significant figures).
An induction motor draws 8.0 A from the mains at a power factor of 0.60 (lagging). Find the wattless component of its current, in amperes.
questions.solution_md: $\sin\phi = \sqrt{1 - 0.60^2} = 0.80$, so the wattless component is $I\sin\phi = 8.0 \times 0.80 = 6.4$ A (the active component is 4.8 A).

marking_scheme.step: sin φ = 0.80; I sin φ = 6.4 A

questions.stem_md: A series circuit with R = 16 Ω, X_L = 45 Ω and X_C = 33 Ω is connected to a 120 V rms supply. Find the average power it takes, in watts.

**Assertion (A):** A large wattless current drawn by a factory increases the energy wasted as heat in the supply cables.

**Reason (R):** Wattless current, being 90° out of phase with the voltage, does no work over a complete cycle.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, but R does not explain A: the cable loss is $I^2R$ for the whole current, wattless part included; R only explains why that part delivers no useful power to the factory — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? As a series LCR circuit is tuned closer and closer to resonance, its power factor rises towards 1.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. $\cos\phi = R/Z$, and $Z$ falls towards $R$ as $X_L - X_C$ approaches zero, so the power factor approaches 1.

questions.stem_md: Older fluorescent-tube fittings limit the current with a choke (a coil of large inductance and very small resistance) instead of a resistor. Explain why, referring to the power factor of the choke.

answer.model_answer_md: A choke’s reactance $\omega L$ is large while its resistance is tiny, so its power factor $R/Z$ is **almost zero**: the current through it is nearly all **wattless**, and it limits the current while taking **almost no power**. A resistor would limit the current equally but would waste $I^2R$ as heat.

questions.solution_md: Power factor near zero.

marking_scheme.step: Large X_L, tiny R: power factor nearly zero
Limits current with negligible power loss; a resistor wastes I²R

questions.stem_md: What is meant by wattless current? Under what condition is the whole current in an AC circuit wattless, and why is a large wattless current still undesirable for the supply company?

answer.model_answer_md: The component $I\sin\phi$ of the current at **90° to the voltage** delivers no average power: it is the **wattless current**. The whole current is wattless in a **purely inductive or purely capacitive** circuit (φ = 90°). It still **heats the supply lines** ($I^2R$ loss), so a power factor near 1 is preferred.

questions.solution_md: I sin φ; φ = 90°; line loss.

marking_scheme.step: I sin φ, in quadrature with V, does no work
Wholly wattless for pure L or C; still causes I²R line loss

questions.stem_md: Show that the average power taken by an AC circuit in which the current lags the voltage by φ is $V_\text{rms}I_\text{rms}\cos\phi$. Hence state the average power taken by an ideal inductor, giving a reason.

answer.model_answer_md: With $v = V_0\sin\omega t$ and $i = I_0\sin(\omega t - \phi)$, the instantaneous power is $p = vi = V_0I_0\sin\omega t\sin(\omega t - \phi) = \dfrac{V_0I_0}{2}[\cos\phi - \cos(2\omega t - \phi)]$. Over a complete cycle $\cos(2\omega t - \phi)$ averages to zero, so $P = \dfrac{V_0I_0}{2}\cos\phi = \dfrac{V_0}{\sqrt2}\dfrac{I_0}{\sqrt2}\cos\phi = V_\text{rms}I_\text{rms}\cos\phi$. For an ideal inductor $\phi = 90^\circ$, so $\cos\phi = 0$ and $P = 0$: the energy it stores in one quarter cycle is returned to the supply in the next.

questions.solution_md: Product-to-sum; the 2ωt term averages to zero.

marking_scheme.step: p = vi written as (V₀I₀/2)[cos φ − cos(2ωt − φ)]
Average: (V₀I₀/2) cos φ = V_rms I_rms cos φ
Ideal inductor: φ = 90°, P = 0, energy returned

questions.stem_md: A lamp rated 60 V, 3.0 A is to be run from 230 V, 50 Hz mains. (a) What resistance placed in series would do, and how much power would it waste? (b) What inductance of a pure choke would do instead? (c) Why is the choke preferred?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The resistor must drop $230 - 60 = 170$ V at 3.0 A: $R = \dfrac{170}{3.0} \approx 56.7$ Ω, wasting $I^2R = 3.0^2 \times 56.67 \approx 510$ W.
(b) Lamp resistance $\dfrac{60}{3.0} = 20$ Ω; total $Z = \dfrac{230}{3.0} \approx 76.67$ Ω; $X_L = \sqrt{76.67^2 - 20^2} \approx 74.0$ Ω; $L = \dfrac{X_L}{2\pi \times 50} \approx 0.236$ H.
(c) A pure choke has power factor zero, so it controls the current while wasting **no power**, unlike the resistor.

questions.solution_md: Series resistor versus choke.

marking_scheme.step: Choke wastes no power (power factor zero)

questions.stem_md: In a series LCR circuit the inductance is doubled and the capacitance halved, the resistance staying the same. The resonant frequency and the Q factor become

options.text_md: twice as large, and unchanged
unchanged, and half as large
half as large, and twice as large
unchanged, and twice as large

questions.solution_md: $f_0 = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$: the product $LC$ is unchanged, so $f_0$ is unchanged. $Q = \dfrac{1}{R}\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{C}}$: $L/C$ becomes 4 times larger, so $Q$ doubles — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A series LCR circuit containing a 25 Ω resistor is connected to a 50 V rms supply whose frequency is adjusted to resonance. The average power it then takes is

options.text_md: zero, since the reactances cancel

questions.solution_md: At resonance $Z = R = 25$ Ω and the power factor is 1, so $I = \dfrac{50}{25} = 2.0$ A and $P = I^2R = 2.0^2 \times 25 = 100$ W — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Find the resonant frequency of a series circuit containing a 2.5 mH inductor and a 0.10 μF capacitor, in kHz (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $LC = 2.5 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.10 \times 10^{-6} = 2.5 \times 10^{-10}$ s², so $f_0 = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}} \approx 1.01 \times 10^{4}$ Hz, i.e. $1.01 \times 10^{4} \times 10^{-3} = 10.1$ kHz.

questions.stem_md: The tuning circuit of a medium-wave radio has a coil of inductance 240 μH. What capacitance tunes it to a station broadcasting at 702 kHz? Give the answer in pF (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: At resonance $C = \dfrac{1}{4\pi^2f^2L} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi^2 \times (702 \times 10^{3})^2 \times 240 \times 10^{-6}} \approx 2.14 \times 10^{-10}$ F, i.e. $2.14 \times 10^{-10} \times 10^{12} = 214$ pF.

questions.stem_md: A series LCR circuit has R = 5.0 Ω, L = 40 mH and C = 0.25 μF. Find its Q factor.
A series resonant circuit has a resonant frequency of 1.2 kHz and a Q factor of 30. Find its bandwidth, in hertz.
questions.solution_md: $Q = \dfrac{f_0}{\Delta f}$, so $\Delta f = \dfrac{1200}{30} = 40$ Hz.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The resonant frequency of a series LCR circuit increases when its resistance is reduced.

**Reason (R):** Reducing the resistance of a series LCR circuit increases the current at resonance.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: $f_0 = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})$ does not depend on R. R is true: at resonance $I_0 = V/R$, which rises as R falls (the peak becomes taller and sharper) — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In an ideal LC circuit, at the instant the capacitor has no charge, the current in the coil is at its greatest.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. When the capacitor is empty all the energy is magnetic, stored in the coil, so the current is at its maximum; it then goes on to charge the capacitor the other way.

questions.stem_md: For a series LCR circuit, the ratio ω₀/Δω of its resonant angular frequency to its bandwidth, which measures how sharp its resonance is, is called its ___ factor.
questions.solution_md: Its **quality** (Q) factor: $Q = \omega_0/\Delta\omega = \omega_0L/R$.

questions.stem_md: A charged capacitor is connected across an ideal inductor. Describe qualitatively how energy is exchanged between them during one cycle, and state what the resistance of a real circuit does to the oscillations.

answer.model_answer_md: The capacitor discharges through the coil: its **electric** energy becomes **magnetic** energy in the coil, all of it when the capacitor is empty and the current greatest. The coil keeps the current flowing and recharges the capacitor the other way; then the process reverses. Resistance turns some energy into **heat** each cycle, so real oscillations **die away**.

questions.solution_md: Electric ⇄ magnetic energy; damping.

marking_scheme.step: Electric energy in C passes to magnetic energy in L and back
Resistance dissipates energy: oscillations die away

questions.stem_md: Two series LCR circuits, X and Y, have the same L and C, but X has R = 10 Ω and Y has R = 50 Ω. Compare their resonant frequencies, currents at resonance on the same supply, and bandwidths. Which is better for a radio tuner, and why?

answer.model_answer_md: Both resonate at the **same** frequency, $1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})$. At resonance $I = V/R$, so X carries **five times** the current of Y. Bandwidth R/L is five times smaller for X, giving a taller, **sharper** peak and a five times larger Q. **X** is better: it picks out one station and rejects its neighbours.

questions.solution_md: Same f₀; I = V/R; Δω = R/L.

marking_scheme.step: Same f₀; X has five times the current
X has one fifth the bandwidth (larger Q): better selectivity

questions.stem_md: A series circuit with L = 0.80 H, C = 5.0 μF and R = 40 Ω is driven by a 20 V rms source of variable frequency. (a) Find the resonant frequency. (b) Find the current and the voltage across the inductor at resonance. (c) Comment on the result of (b).

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\omega_0 = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{0.80 \times 5.0 \times 10^{-6}}} = 500$ rad s$^{-1}$, so $f_0 = \dfrac{500}{2\pi} \approx 79.6$ Hz.
(b) $I = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{20}{40} = 0.50$ A; $X_L = \omega_0L = 500 \times 0.80 = 400$ Ω, so $V_L = 0.50 \times 400 = 200$ V.
(c) $V_L$ (and $V_C$) is **ten times** the supply voltage: the two cancel each other, and $Q = \omega_0L/R = 10$ is the voltage magnification at resonance.

questions.stem_md: At the instant the magnetic flux through the turning coil of an AC generator is greatest, the emf induced in the coil is

options.text_md: greatest, because the flux is greatest
half its peak value
zero, because the flux is not changing at that instant
greatest, because the sides of the coil are then moving along the field

questions.solution_md: $e = -\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}$. With $\Phi = NBA\cos\omega t$, the flux is greatest when $\cos\omega t = \pm1$, where its rate of change, and so the emf $NBA\omega\sin\omega t$, is zero; the sides of the coil are then moving along the field and cut no lines — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A generator coil is rewound with half as many turns of the same area and is then turned twice as fast in the same field. Compared with before, its peak emf and the frequency of its output are

options.text_md: doubled, and doubled
halved, and unchanged
unchanged, and unchanged
unchanged, and doubled

questions.solution_md: $e_0 = NBA\omega$: halving $N$ and doubling $\omega$ leaves $e_0$ unchanged. The frequency equals the number of turns of the coil per second, so it doubles — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The coil of a two-pole AC generator in a small hydro-power station turns at 3000 revolutions per minute. The frequency of its output is

options.text_md: 100 Hz
314 Hz
50 Hz

questions.solution_md: 3000 revolutions per minute is $\dfrac{3000}{60} = 50$ revolutions per second, and the emf goes through one cycle per revolution: 50 Hz — option (d).

questions.stem_md: What is the main reason why electric power is generated and distributed as alternating current rather than direct current?

options.text_md: AC voltages can be stepped up and down efficiently by transformers, so power can be sent at high voltage with small line losses
AC is less dangerous than DC at the same rms voltage
AC can be stored in batteries more easily than DC
AC needs no insulation on its cables

questions.solution_md: Transformers work only with a changing current. Transmitting at high voltage means a small current and small $I^2R$ losses; the voltage is stepped down again near the consumer — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A coil of 250 turns, each of area 0.012 m², turns about an axis perpendicular to a uniform field of 0.35 T. How many revolutions per second must it make to give a peak emf of 300 V? (3 significant figures)
questions.solution_md: $e_0 = NBA\omega$, so $\omega = \dfrac{e_0}{NBA} = \dfrac{300}{250 \times 0.35 \times 0.012} \approx 285.7$ rad s$^{-1}$, and $n = \dfrac{\omega}{2\pi} = \dfrac{285.7}{2\pi} = 45.5$ revolutions per second.

questions.stem_md: A rectangular coil of 60 turns, each 10 cm × 5.0 cm, rotates at 1500 revolutions per minute about an axis perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.80 T. Find the rms value of the emf induced in it, in volts (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $A = 0.10 \times 0.050 = 5.0 \times 10^{-3}$ m²; $\omega = 2\pi \times \dfrac{1500}{60} \approx 157.1$ rad s$^{-1}$; $e_0 = NBA\omega = 60 \times 0.80 \times 5.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 157.1 \approx 37.70$ V; $e_\text{rms} = \dfrac{37.70}{\sqrt2} = 26.7$ V.

questions.stem_md: The peak emf of an AC generator is 240 V. Find the instantaneous emf at the moment the plane of its coil makes an angle of 30° with the magnetic field, in volts (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $e = e_0\sin\theta$, where θ is the angle between the **normal** to the coil and the field. With the plane at 30° to the field, the normal is at 60°, so $e = 240 \times 0.866 = 208$ V.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The emf of an AC generator with slip rings has a frequency equal to the number of rotations its coil makes each second.

**Reason (R):** The emf of an AC generator is greatest at the instant the flux through its coil is greatest.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Assertion is false and Reason is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: the emf $NBA\omega\sin\omega t$ goes through one cycle per rotation. R is false: the emf is greatest when the flux is zero (plane along the field), where the flux changes fastest — option (c).

questions.stem_md: State two differences between alternating current and direct current, and give one advantage of each over the other.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) AC **reverses direction** periodically (50 times a second in India) and its value keeps changing; DC flows in **one direction**, usually steady. (ii) AC voltage is easily **stepped up or down by transformers**; DC voltage is not. **Advantage of AC:** efficient long-distance transmission at high voltage. **Advantage of DC:** it can **charge batteries** and is used for electroplating.

questions.solution_md: Direction; transformability; uses.

questions.stem_md: State the principle of an AC generator. Name its main parts and give the function of the slip rings and the brushes. Explain why the emf it produces alternates.

answer.model_answer_md: **Principle:** electromagnetic induction — when a coil turns in a magnetic field, the flux linked with it changes and an emf is induced. **Parts:** armature coil, field magnet, slip rings and carbon brushes. The **slip rings**, fixed to the axle and joined to the coil’s ends, turn with it; the **brushes** press on them and connect the turning coil to the external circuit. Every half turn each side of the coil reverses its direction of motion across the field, so the induced emf **reverses**: it varies as NBAω sin ωt.

questions.solution_md: EMI; slip rings and brushes; reversal every half turn.

Parts and the function of slip rings and brushes

questions.stem_md: (a) Show that the rms value of a sinusoidal current $i = I_0\sin\omega t$ is $I_0/\sqrt2$. [2] (b) Write the mean value of this current over a half cycle and explain why its mean over a full cycle is not used. [1] (c) A 25 μF capacitor is connected to 230 V, 50 Hz mains. Find its reactance and the rms and peak values of the current. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The rms value is the square root of the mean of $i^2$ over a cycle. $\overline{i^2} = \dfrac{1}{T}\int_0^T I_0^2\sin^2\omega t\,dt = \dfrac{I_0^2}{T}\int_0^T \dfrac{1 - \cos 2\omega t}{2}\,dt = \dfrac{I_0^2}{2}$, because $\cos 2\omega t$ averages to zero over a cycle. So $I_\text{rms} = I_0/\sqrt2$.

(b) $\bar I = 2I_0/\pi \approx 0.637\,I_0$ over a half cycle. Over a full cycle the positive and negative halves cancel, so the mean is always zero and gives no information.

(c) $X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi \times 50 \times 25 \times 10^{-6}} \approx 127.3$ Ω; $I_\text{rms} = \dfrac{230}{127.3} \approx 1.81$ A; $I_0 = \sqrt2 \times 1.81 \approx 2.55$ A.

questions.solution_md: Mean of sin² = 1/2; 2I₀/π; X_C = 1/(2πfC).

marking_scheme.step: Mean of i² over a cycle = I₀²/2

questions.stem_md: (a) Describe the phasor diagram of a series LCR circuit and use it to obtain the impedance of the circuit. [2] (b) A 55 Ω resistor, a 0.25 H inductor and a 30 μF capacitor are joined in series across 230 V, 50 Hz mains. Find (i) the impedance, (ii) the rms current and whether it leads or lags the voltage, (iii) the power factor and the average power. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The current $I$ is common, so it is the reference. $V_R = IR$ lies along $I$, $V_L = IX_L$ is 90° ahead and $V_C = IX_C$ is 90° behind. $V_L$ and $V_C$ combine to $V_L - V_C$ at right angles to $V_R$, so $V^2 = V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2$ and $Z = V/I = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$, with $\tan\phi = (X_L - X_C)/R$.

(b)(i) $X_L = 2\pi \times 50 \times 0.25 \approx 78.54$ Ω, $X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi \times 50 \times 30 \times 10^{-6}} \approx 106.1$ Ω, so $Z = \sqrt{55^2 + (78.54 - 106.1)^2} \approx 61.52$ Ω.
(ii) $I = \dfrac{230}{61.52} \approx 3.74$ A. $X_C > X_L$, so the circuit is capacitive and the current **leads**, by $\phi \approx 26.6^\circ$.
(iii) $\cos\phi = \dfrac{R}{Z} = \dfrac{55}{61.52} \approx 0.894$; $P = I^2R \approx 3.74^2 \times 55 \approx 769$ W.

questions.solution_md: Phasor sum; reactances; Z; I; cos φ = R/Z; P = I²R.

marking_scheme.step: Phasor diagram described: V_R along I, V_L ahead, V_C behind

questions.stem_md: (a) Define power factor and wattless current. [1] (b) Why is a choke coil preferred to a resistor for limiting an alternating current? [1] (c) A coil draws 5.0 A from 230 V, 50 Hz mains and consumes 400 W. Find (i) its power factor, (ii) its resistance and impedance, (iii) its inductance. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The power factor is $\cos\phi = P/(V_\text{rms}I_\text{rms})$, equal to $R/Z$ for a series circuit. Wattless current is the component $I\sin\phi$ of the current at 90° to the voltage, which delivers no average power.

(b) A choke has a large reactance and almost no resistance, so its power factor is nearly zero: it limits the current while wasting almost no energy, whereas a resistor wastes $I^2R$ as heat.

(c)(i) $\cos\phi = \dfrac{P}{VI} = \dfrac{400}{230 \times 5.0} \approx 0.348$.
(ii) $R = \dfrac{P}{I^2} = \dfrac{400}{25} = 16$ Ω; $Z = \dfrac{230}{5.0} = 46$ Ω.
(iii) $X_L = \sqrt{46^2 - 16^2} = \sqrt{1860} \approx 43.13$ Ω, so $L = \dfrac{X_L}{2\pi \times 50} \approx 0.137$ H.

questions.solution_md: cos φ = P/VI; R = P/I²; Z = V/I; X_L from Z and R.

Choke: power factor nearly zero, negligible loss

questions.stem_md: (a) State the condition for resonance in a series LCR circuit and obtain an expression for its resonant frequency. [1] (b) A circuit with L = 0.20 H, C = 2.0 μF and R = 25 Ω is driven by a 10 V rms source of variable frequency. Find (i) the resonant frequency, (ii) the rms current at resonance, (iii) the Q factor and the bandwidth in hertz. [3] (c) Describe, without equations, what happens to the energy in an LC circuit after its charged capacitor is connected across the coil. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Resonance occurs when $X_L = X_C$, i.e. $\omega L = \dfrac{1}{\omega C}$, giving $\omega_0 = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$ and $f_0 = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$; then $Z = R$.

(b)(i) $\omega_0 = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{0.20 \times 2.0 \times 10^{-6}}} \approx 1581$ rad s$^{-1}$, so $f_0 \approx 252$ Hz.
(ii) $I = \dfrac{V}{R} = \dfrac{10}{25} = 0.40$ A.
(iii) $Q = \dfrac{\omega_0L}{R} \approx \dfrac{1581 \times 0.20}{25} \approx 12.6$; $\Delta\omega = \dfrac{R}{L} = \dfrac{25}{0.20} = 125$ rad s$^{-1}$, so $\Delta f = \dfrac{125}{2\pi} \approx 19.9$ Hz.

(c) The capacitor discharges through the coil, so its electric energy turns into magnetic energy in the coil; the coil then recharges the capacitor the opposite way, and the energy keeps passing back and forth, slowly lost as heat in any resistance.

questions.solution_md: X_L = X_C; I = V/R; Q = ω₀L/R; Δω = R/L.

marking_scheme.step: Energy exchanged between C and L; damped by resistance

questions.stem_md: (a) Explain, with a labelled diagram (described in words), the construction and working of an AC generator. [2] (b) Derive the expression for the emf induced in its coil as it turns with angular speed ω. [1] (c) A coil of 120 turns, each of area 0.025 m², turns at 50 revolutions per second in a uniform field of 0.25 T. Find the peak and rms emf, and the emf 1/600 s after the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) An armature coil of many turns on a soft-iron core is mounted on an axle between the poles of a strong field magnet, its axis of rotation perpendicular to the field. Its two ends are joined to two slip rings on the axle; carbon brushes press on the rings and lead to the external circuit. A turbine turns the coil, the flux through it changes continuously, and an alternating emf is induced (electromagnetic induction).

(b) If the normal to the coil is along B at $t = 0$, then at time $t$ the angle is $\omega t$ and $\Phi = NBA\cos\omega t$; so $e = -\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} = NBA\omega\sin\omega t = e_0\sin\omega t$.

(c) $\omega = 2\pi \times 50 \approx 314.2$ rad s$^{-1}$; $e_0 = NBA\omega = 120 \times 0.25 \times 0.025 \times 314.2 \approx 235.6$ V; $e_\text{rms} = e_0/\sqrt2 \approx 166.6$ V. At $t = \dfrac{1}{600}$ s, $\omega t = \dfrac{2\pi \times 50}{600} = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$, so $e = e_0\sin 30^\circ \approx 117.8$ V.
